title: Bladder, bowel, catheter and stoma care
blurb: Support continence, care for urinary catheters to NICE standards, manage constipation, diarrhoea and retention, and look after stomas.
question: Mr Foster, 77, has a long-term urinary catheter in a nursing home. A carer has hung his drainage bag on the bed frame at mattress height and asks whether a weekly bladder washout would stop infections. What should the nurse advise?

teach.h: Bladder and bowel care is a fundamental
teach.body: The NMC Code names bladder and bowel care among the fundamentals of care. Continence problems are common, embarrassing and often treatable, and they affect skin, mood, sleep, falls and dignity. In plain English: ask about bladder and bowels as routinely as you check a pulse, record what you find accurately, offer privacy and timely help to the toilet, and look for causes rather than just reaching for pads.
teach.cite: NMC Code (2015, updated 2018) clause 1 note; NICE NG249 (continence in falls assessment)

head: Point
Guidance
rows: Consider alternatives; intermittent preferred where practical
Aseptic; balloon 10 mL sterile water in adults, 3–5 mL in children
Sterile closed drainage system or catheter valve
Hand hygiene and new non-sterile gloves before touching it
Below the bladder and not touching the floor
Must not be used to prevent infection
Review the need regularly; remove as soon as possible
teach.caption: NICE CG139 (updated 2017) section 1.2. Overnight: use a link system so the original closed system stays intact. Samples: from the sampling port, aseptically.

teach.body: The nurse explains that the bag must hang below the level of his bladder (but off the floor) so urine drains and cannot flow back, and moves it to a stand. She explains that NICE CG139 says bladder washouts must not be used to prevent infection. She reviews whether he still needs a long-term catheter, checks the closed system is unbroken, and reminds staff about hand hygiene and clean gloves before handling the catheter and daily meatal hygiene.

teach.caption: NHS England Bristol Stool Chart (2023): types 1–2 can indicate constipation, 3–4 are easiest to pass, 5–6 may indicate diarrhoea, and type 7 may mean illness or overflow from faecal impaction.

steps.label: Lifestyle
steps.sub: Fibre towards 30 g/day, fluids if dehydrated, activity

steps.label: Toilet routine
steps.sub: Unhurried, privacy, respond to the urge, help to access

steps.label: Laxatives
steps.sub: Bulk-forming first; osmotic if still hard; stimulant if soft but hard to pass

teach.caption: Faecal loading or impaction may need suppositories or enemas as prescribed. Type 7 stool in an immobile, constipated person can be overflow, not true diarrhoea.

children.label: Isolate and sample
children.sub: Single room, stool sample, soap and water hand hygiene

children.label: Overflow
children.sub: Assess for impaction; treat the cause

children.label: Fluids and skin
children.sub: Fluid balance, barrier care, review laxatives

teach.caption: NIPCM: use soap and water (not alcohol rub) for hand hygiene when caring for people with vomiting or diarrhoea or suspected C. difficile or norovirus.

rows.label: Output
values: None for much longer than normal

rows.label: Skin
values: Sore from leaks or poor fit

teach.caption: NHS ileostomy and colostomy information: measure the stoma regularly so the bag fits well; ileostomy output is higher and looser, so watch for dehydration.

items: Suspect it when someone cannot pass urine, passes small amounts often, has lower abdominal discomfort or is newly restless or confused.
Common triggers: after surgery or anaesthesia, opioids, constipation, immobility.
Assess bladder volume (for example with a bladder scanner, if trained) and escalate.
In people who cannot say they are uncomfortable, a full bladder is a common, easily missed cause of agitation or new confusion.

teach.text: Bladder washouts do not prevent catheter infection (CG139 says they must not be used for that), and catheter bags lying on the floor or hung above the bladder both raise infection risk. Also, 'diarrhoea' in a constipated, bedbound person may be overflow around impacted stool: treating it with antidiarrhoeals makes things worse.

items: Catheters: alternatives first; aseptic insertion; closed system; bag below bladder and off the floor; no washouts to prevent infection; review and remove early (CG139).
Hand hygiene and clean non-sterile gloves before handling a catheter; samples from the sampling port.
Bristol types 1–2 constipation, 3–4 normal, 5–7 loose; type 7 can be overflow.
Constipation: causes, lifestyle, routine, stepwise laxatives; no bulk-forming for opioid constipation.
Stoma: pink or red and moist; dark or black, no output or high output and dehydration need urgent review.

summary: You can now care for urinary catheters to NICE CG139, use the Bristol Stool Chart, manage constipation stepwise, respond safely to new diarrhoea or suspected retention, and recognise stoma problems that need urgent review.

A.q: Mrs Hale, 82, has an indwelling catheter in a care home. Where should her drainage bag be positioned?
options: Level with her bladder on the bed frame
On the floor beside the bed for stability
Below her bladder and off the floor
Above her bladder to slow urine flow
A.why: NICE CG139: drainage bags should be positioned below the level of the bladder and should not be in contact with the floor.

whyNot.0: At bladder level urine may not drain and can flow back.
whyNot.1: Contact with the floor increases contamination risk.
whyNot.3: Above the bladder allows reflux of urine and raises infection risk.

A.q: A healthcare support worker asks whether a routine bladder washout would prevent infection in Mr Lake's long-term catheter. According to NICE CG139, what is the answer?
options: Yes, if done weekly with sterile saline
Yes, if the catheter has been in for over a month
No, washouts are not used to prevent infection
No, but daily antibiotic cover should be given
A.why: CG139: bladder instillations or washouts must not be used to prevent catheter-associated infections.

whyNot.0: Frequency or fluid does not change the CG139 position.
whyNot.1: Duration of catheterisation does not make washouts preventive.
whyNot.3: Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended and drives resistance.

A.q: Mr Bose, 68, reports changes in his bowel habit since starting a new medicine, alternating between hard pellets and loose stools. Which tool helps record his stool type consistently?
options: The Bristol Stool Chart
The 'MUST' screening tool
A fluid balance chart
The Waterlow score
A.why: The Bristol Stool Chart classifies stool into seven types, from separate hard lumps (type 1) to entirely liquid (type 7).

whyNot.2: A fluid balance chart records volumes in and out, not stool form.

B.q: Mrs Penn, 85, on a medical ward, has had three episodes of watery stool (Bristol type 7) since this morning with no obvious cause. She started antibiotics 3 days ago. What should the nurse do first?
options: Give loperamide and keep her in her bay
Isolate her in a side room and send a stool sample
Wait for a fourth episode before taking further action
Use alcohol handrub after every contact with her
B.why: Unexplained diarrhoea after antibiotics may be C. difficile or another infection: isolate promptly (SICPs patient placement), send a stool sample and use soap and water for hand hygiene (NIPCM).

whyNot.0: Antidiarrhoeals can be harmful in infective diarrhoea and leaving her in a bay risks spread.
whyNot.2: Delaying isolation risks transmission to others.
whyNot.3: Alcohol rub does not kill C. difficile spores; soap and water is needed.

B.q: Mrs Ivy, 74, had a hip replacement 8 hours ago. She has not passed urine since surgery, feels she needs to go but cannot, and has lower abdominal discomfort. What should the nurse do next?
options: Encourage oral fluids and recheck in 4 hours
Give prescribed analgesia and reassess later
Insert a catheter without further assessment
Assess her bladder volume with a scanner
B.why: This picture suggests urinary retention after surgery. Assessing bladder volume confirms it and guides escalation and catheterisation if needed.

whyNot.0: More fluid into an already full bladder increases discomfort and delays diagnosis.
whyNot.1: Analgesia may mask the problem without treating the cause.
whyNot.2: Catheterisation is invasive; CG139 asks that alternatives and need are assessed first.

B.q: Mr Ali, 66, had a colostomy formed 2 days ago. On inspection the stoma is dark purple-black and dry. Yesterday it was red and moist. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Report it urgently to the surgical team
Apply a barrier cream and recheck tomorrow
Cut the appliance larger to relieve pressure
Record it as normal post-operative bruising
B.why: A healthy stoma is pink or red and moist. A purple or black stoma suggests its blood supply is compromised and needs urgent surgical review.

whyNot.1: Barrier cream does not address a compromised blood supply.
whyNot.2: Changing the appliance does not treat ischaemia and delays review.
whyNot.3: Darkening is not normal and must not be dismissed.

C.q: Mr Cole, 88, is bedbound with dementia. He has had no formed stool for 7 days and is now leaking small amounts of liquid stool (type 7). His abdomen is distended. What is the most likely explanation and action?
options: Infective diarrhoea; start loperamide straight away
Overflow around impaction; assess and escalate
Normal ageing of the bowel; record and observe
Laxative excess; stop his laxatives and reassess
C.why: Liquid stool after days without a formed stool, with a distended abdomen, suggests overflow from faecal impaction (NHS Bristol chart: type 7 may be overflow). Assess and escalate for treatment such as enemas as prescribed.

whyNot.2: This is not normal ageing and needs treatment.
whyNot.3: No laxative excess is described; he has not passed a formed stool for a week.

C.q: Mrs Grey, 72, has an indwelling catheter. A urine sample is requested. How should it be obtained?
options: From the drainage bag tap into a sterile pot
From the sampling port using aseptic technique
By disconnecting the bag and catching urine
From the next void after removing the catheter
C.why: NICE CG139: urine samples must be obtained from the sampling port using an aseptic technique.

whyNot.0: Urine in the bag has been standing and gives a contaminated, unreliable sample.
whyNot.2: Breaking the closed system raises infection risk.
whyNot.3: Removing a catheter just to sample is unnecessary.

C.q: Mr Reed, 59, has a new ileostomy. On day 4 his output is very high and watery, he feels tired and has a dry mouth. What is the priority?
options: Reassure him that a high output is expected
Advise him to drink less to slow the output
Assess for dehydration and escalate
Change the appliance to a larger closed bag
C.why: NHS ileostomy information: high output makes dehydration likely; tiredness and dry mouth are warning signs. Assess fluid status and escalate.

whyNot.0: Very high output with symptoms is not reassuring.
whyNot.3: Changing the bag does not address fluid loss.

reteach.title: Keep it closed, keep it low, keep it short
reteach.question: How can three short rules cover most of urinary catheter care?

blocks.body: Closed: the catheter and bag form a sterile closed system; break it as little as possible, use the sampling port and a link bag overnight. Low: the bag sits below the bladder so urine drains away and cannot flow back, but off the floor. Short: every day with a catheter adds infection risk, so ask daily whether it is still needed and remove it as soon as possible.

blocks.text: Washouts are not part of keeping a catheter clean: CG139 says they must not be used to prevent infection.

explain.body: Use an indwelling catheter only after alternatives are considered; intermittent catheterisation is preferred where practical. Insert aseptically; balloon 10 mL sterile water in adults (3–5 mL children). Review need regularly and remove as soon as possible.

test.q: Under NICE CG139, how much sterile water is generally used to inflate an adult catheter balloon?
options: 5 mL
20 mL
10 mL
30 mL
test.why: CG139: in general the balloon is inflated with 10 mL of sterile water in adults and 3–5 mL in children.

whyNot.0: 5 mL is within the children's range.
whyNot.1: 20 mL is double the general adult volume.
whyNot.3: 30 mL is far above the CG139 volume.

explain.body: Closed system. Hand hygiene and new clean non-sterile gloves before handling. Bag below bladder, off floor; link bag overnight; empty often enough to keep flow and prevent reflux. Samples from the port. No washouts to prevent infection.

test.q: What should a nurse do before emptying a catheter bag?
options: Put on sterile gloves
Clean hands and wear new clean gloves
Disconnect the bag to check the flow
Instil saline to flush the catheter first
test.why: CG139: decontaminate hands and wear a new pair of clean, non-sterile gloves before manipulating a catheter.

whyNot.0: Sterile gloves are for insertion, not routine handling.
whyNot.3: Instillations are not used routinely and break the system.

explain.body: Bristol 1–2 constipation, 3–4 ideal, 5–7 loose; type 7 can be overflow. Constipation: causes, fibre, fluids if dehydrated, activity, toilet routine and privacy, then stepwise laxatives (not bulk-forming for opioids).

test.q: Which Bristol Stool Chart types are easiest to pass?
options: Types 1 and 2
Types 5 and 6
Type 7 on its own
Types 3 and 4
test.why: NHS England Bristol Stool Chart: types 3 and 4 are the easiest to pass; type 4 is ideal.

whyNot.2: Type 7 is entirely liquid and may indicate illness or overflow.

explain.body: Healthy: pink or red, moist, not painful. Measure regularly so the appliance fits and skin stays intact. Urgent: purple or black, no output for much longer than normal, lots of blood, signs of dehydration (especially with an ileostomy).

test.q: Why should a stoma be measured regularly?
options: To decide when to reverse it
To check for a parastomal hernia
To calculate the daily output volume
So the bag fits and skin is intact
test.why: NHS ileostomy advice: measure the stoma regularly to make sure the bag fits well and prevent skin damage from leaks.

whyNot.0: Reversal is a surgical decision, not based on stoma size.
whyNot.1: A parastomal hernia shows as a bulge in the skin around the stoma and is reported if noticed; routine measuring is done to keep the appliance fitting.
whyNot.2: Output is measured from the bag, not the stoma size.
